title: Present perfect 2 (I have done)
subtitle: Have you ever ... ? / It's the first time ...
summary: Use the present perfect for a period that continues until now (ever, never, so far, this week) and in 'It's the first time something has happened'.

lesson.heading: Study this conversation
lesson.text: *Dave:* Have you travelled a lot, Jane? *Jane:* Yes, I've been to lots of places. *Dave:* Really? Have you ever been to China? *Jane:* Yes, I've been to China twice. *Dave:* What about India? *Jane:* No, I haven't been to India. When we talk about a period of time that continues from the past until now, we use the present perfect. Dave and Jane are talking about the places Jane has visited in her life - a period that continues until now.

examples.text: **Have you ever been** to China?
Yes, **I've been** to China twice.
No, **I haven't been** to India.

lesson.heading: ever, never, three times ...
lesson.text: In the same way we use the present perfect for experiences in a person's life up to now. **been (to)** = visited.

examples.text: **Have you ever eaten** caviar?
**We've never had** a car.
I don't know what the film is about. **I haven't seen** it.
Susan really loves that book. **She's read** it three times.
It's a really boring movie. It's the most boring movie **I've ever seen**.
**I've never been** to Canada. Have you been there?

lesson.heading: A period that continues until now
lesson.text: The speakers here are also talking about a period that continues until now: **recently**, **in the last few days**, **so far**, **since I arrived**, **for a long time** etc.

examples.text: **Have you heard** anything from Ben recently?
**I've met** a lot of people in the last few days.
Everything is going well. **There haven't been** any problems so far.
The weather is bad here. **It's rained** every day since I arrived.
examples.note: = from when I arrived until now

examples.text: It's good to see you again. **We haven't seen** each other for a long time.

lesson.heading: today, this evening, this year
lesson.text: In the same way we use the present perfect with **today**, **this evening**, **this year** etc. when these periods are not finished at the time of speaking.

examples.text: **I've drunk** four cups of coffee today.
**Have you had** a holiday this year?
**I haven't seen** Tom this morning. Have you?

lesson.heading: It's the first time something has happened
lesson.text: Don is having a driving lesson. It's his first lesson. We say: It's the first time **he has driven** a car (not drives). or **He hasn't driven** a car before. or **He has never driven** a car before.

examples.text: It's the first time **he has driven** a car.
**He hasn't driven** a car before. / **He has never driven** a car before.
Sarah has lost her passport again. This is the second time this **has happened**.
Andy is phoning his girlfriend again. It's the third time **he's phoned** her this evening.

lesson.text: Time words that reach up to now - ever, never, so far, recently, today, this week - point to the present perfect.

exercises.prompt: You ask people about things they have done. Ask about California.
exercises.answer: Have you ever been to California?
exercises.explanation: Have + subject + ever + past participle. been to = visited.

exercises.prompt: Match A's questions with B's answers.

pairs.right: I've no idea. I've never met her.
Yes, we haven't had any problems so far.
Yes, but I haven't played for ages.
I don't know. I haven't read it.
I've no idea. I've never been there.
I don't know. I've never tried it.

exercises.explanation: today is not finished, so present perfect: haven't eaten.

exercises.prompt: 'Are you enjoying your holiday?' 'Yes, it's the best holiday ___ for a long time.'
exercises.explanation: for a long time = a period up to now: the best holiday I've had.

exercises.statement: It's a really boring movie. It's the most boring movie I've ever seen.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Superlative + ever + present perfect: the most boring movie I've ever seen.

exercises.prompt: 'I hear your car broke down again yesterday.' 'Yes, it's the second time ___ this month.'
exercises.explanation: It's the second time + present perfect: it's happened.

exercises.prompt: 'Mike was late for work again today.' 'Again? He ___ late every day this week.'
exercises.explanation: this week is not finished yet: He's been late every day this week.

exercises.prompt: Jack is driving a car for the first time. He's very nervous. It's the first time he ___ a car.
exercises.explanation: It's the first time + present perfect: he has driven (not drives).

exercises.statement: Sarah has lost her passport again. This is the second time this happens.
exercises.explanation: This is the second time this has happened. After 'the first/second time' we use the present perfect.

exercises.prompt: Some children at the zoo are looking at a giraffe. They've never seen one before. It's the first time ___ a giraffe.
exercises.explanation: It's the first time + present perfect: they've seen.

exercises.prompt: Sue is riding a horse. She doesn't look very confident or comfortable. She ___ a horse before.
exercises.explanation: First experience: She has never ridden a horse before (past participle ridden).

exercises.prompt: Ask a friend about the most beautiful place in their life so far.
exercises.answer: What's the most beautiful place you've ever visited?
